prompt: In `abandon.go`, what made the client give up after 100 milliseconds?
hint: Look at how the request was built.

choices.text: `http.DefaultClient` has a timeout of 100 ms
choices.why: The default client has no timeout at all; the limit came from the request's context.

choices.text: Its context ended at 100 ms
choices.why: Right: `http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, …)` with a 100 ms timeout.

choices.text: The server closed the connection
choices.why: It was the other way round: the client left, and the server noticed.

choices.text: `net.Listen` limits connections to 100 ms on 127.0.0.1
choices.why: The listener sets no time limit on anything.

prompt: The client's error said `context deadline exceeded` and the server's line said `context canceled`. Why the different reasons?
hint: What does the server actually observe?

choices.text: The server's clock runs behind the client's
choices.why: They are one process with one clock.

choices.text: `r.Context()` has its own deadline of two seconds
choices.why: The two seconds are the handler's `time.After`, not a deadline on the context.

choices.text: The server sees the connection close, not the client's reason
choices.why: Right. It cancels the request's context because the client left; why it left never crosses the wire.

choices.text: A server always reports canceled, whatever happens
choices.why: When the handler finished normally there was no error at all.

prompt: A handler ignores `r.Context()` and always spends two seconds building its report. Clients give up after 100 ms under load. What happens to the server?
hint: Who is the work for, once the client has gone?

choices.text: It works for nobody and falls behind
choices.why: Right. Every timed-out request still costs its full two seconds.

choices.text: The runtime stops the handler when the client leaves
choices.why: Nothing stops a handler from outside; it has to look at its context.

choices.text: The client's timeout makes the handler panic
choices.why: No panic: the handler simply carries on, which is the problem.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because clients retry
choices.why: Retries add more work, so the backlog grows faster.

prompt: A handler replies at once and starts a goroutine to send a confirmation e-mail that may take ten seconds. Which context should the goroutine use?

choices.text: `r.Context()`, so the e-mail is tied to the request
choices.why: That context ends when the handler returns, which here is at once, cancelling the e-mail.

choices.text: `context.WithoutCancel`, plus a timeout
choices.why: Right: keep the request's values, drop its ending, and bound the e-mail separately.

choices.text: A context stored in the server struct
choices.why: Lesson 11 gave the reason not to keep contexts in structs.

choices.text: No context, since the e-mail is in a goroutine
choices.why: A goroutine is exactly where a context is needed, to be able to stop it.

prompt: The method of `*http.Request` that returns the context the server gives each handler is `r.___()`.
hint: The handler in `abandon.go` waited on it in a `select`.

prompt: Why did `nodb.go` stop at `open: sql: unknown driver "postgres"`?

choices.text: The query's SQL had a syntax error
choices.why: The query never ran; the program stopped at `sql.Open`.

choices.text: The two-second timeout ran out
choices.why: The failure came before any query, and instantly.

choices.text: No driver is registered; the standard library ships none
choices.why: Right: "No database drivers are included in the Go standard library."

choices.text: PostgreSQL refused the user `ana`
choices.why: Nothing reached a database; there is none on this machine.

prompt: What context does `db.Query(...)`, without `Context` in its name, use?
hint: Its documentation says it in one sentence.

choices.text: The context of the goroutine that calls it
choices.why: Goroutines have no context of their own; a context is a value passed by hand.

choices.text: `context.Background()`, which never ends
choices.why: Right: "Query uses context.Background internally." A query made with it waits as long as the database takes.

choices.text: A context with the driver's default timeout
choices.why: The documentation names `context.Background`, which has no timeout.

choices.text: The last context passed to `QueryContext`
choices.why: `*sql.DB` keeps no context between calls.

prompt: A function loops over `rows.Next()` and returns what it collected, without calling `rows.Err()`. The request's context ends halfway through the rows. What does the caller get?
hint: Where does an error that ends the iteration show up?

choices.text: A panic from `rows.Next()`
choices.why: `rows.Next()` returns false; it does not panic.

choices.text: The context's error, from `rows.Scan`
choices.why: `Scan` is not called once `Next` has returned false.

choices.text: An empty slice and an error
choices.why: The rows read before the end are in the slice, and without `rows.Err()` there is no error.

choices.text: Half the rows and a nil error
choices.why: Right. The error is only in `rows.Err()`, so skipping it passes half a result off as all of it.

prompt: Which of these does `nodb.go` show, even though it never reaches a database? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The query takes the context first, through `QueryContext`
choices.why: Yes, the same convention as lesson 11.

choices.text: `orders` derives a child with its own limit
choices.why: Yes, two seconds, and a caller with less time still wins.

choices.text: How PostgreSQL cancels a running query
choices.why: Nothing here reached PostgreSQL. That is for a course with a database, `go-back`.

choices.text: How long the query took
choices.why: No query ran.

prompt: In `demo.sh`, the request for `/late` came a tenth of a second after the interrupt. What did `curl` get?

choices.text: A slow answer, delivered after the first
choices.why: Only `/report` was answered; it was already inside.

choices.text: `Couldn't connect to server`
choices.why: Right. `Shutdown` closes the listener at once, so nobody was listening.

choices.text: An HTTP 503 from the server
choices.why: There was no server listening to send one.

choices.text: A reset in the middle of the reply
choices.why: It never connected, so there was no reply to cut.

prompt: Put what `shutdown.go` printed, and what happened around it, in order.
hint: The door closes before the work inside is finished.

prompt: Why does `shutdown.go` give `Shutdown` a new context of five seconds instead of the signal context `ctx`?
hint: What state is `ctx` in at that moment?

choices.text: `Shutdown` refuses contexts made by `signal.NotifyContext`
choices.why: It accepts any context; the issue is that this one has ended.

choices.text: Five seconds is the time a signal takes to arrive
choices.why: The signal had already arrived; that is why the code reached this line.

choices.text: `ctx` has already ended
choices.why: Right. A fresh context gives the requests inside up to five seconds to finish.

choices.text: To reset `GOMAXPROCS` before the program exits
choices.why: Contexts have nothing to do with `GOMAXPROCS`.

prompt: A platform sends `SIGTERM` and kills the process outright 10 seconds later. A team sets the `Shutdown` limit to 30 seconds. What goes wrong?
hint: The limit is a promise to whoever sent the signal.

choices.text: Nothing: a longer limit is safer
choices.why: Longer than the platform's patience means the platform decides, mid-request.

choices.text: Requests still running at 10 s die mid-reply
choices.why: Right. The limit has to be shorter than the platform's wait for it to mean anything.

choices.text: `Shutdown` returns an error at once
choices.why: It would wait happily; it is the platform that does not.

choices.text: `SIGTERM` is ignored by `signal.NotifyContext`
choices.why: `shutdown.go` lists `syscall.SIGTERM` among its signals.

prompt: Match each piece of the standard library with what it does with a context.
hint: One makes a context, three take one.

pairs.right: ends a context when a signal arrives
lets a client give up on a request
tells a handler its client has gone
bounds the wait for requests in flight

right_distractors: cancels every running handler at once

prompt: During a `Shutdown`, a handler is in the middle of a five-minute export and never looks at `r.Context()`. The `Shutdown` limit is five seconds. What happens?

choices.text: `Shutdown` cancels the handler after five seconds
choices.why: `Shutdown` waits for handlers; it does not cancel them.

choices.text: The export finishes, and `Shutdown` waits all five minutes
choices.why: `Shutdown` stops waiting when its own context ends, after five seconds.

choices.text: It gives up at five seconds, export unfinished
choices.why: Right. It returns its context's error and `main` goes on to exit, killing the export halfway.

choices.text: The export moves to another server
choices.why: Nothing in the standard library moves work between processes.

prompt: Which of the three cases in this lesson was NOT run end to end on the lab machine?

choices.text: The abandoned HTTP request
choices.why: It ran: both lines, client and server, are a capture.

choices.text: The query with a deadline
choices.why: Right. There is no database here; the code compiled and stopped at the missing driver.

choices.text: The graceful shutdown
choices.why: It ran, signal and all, through `demo.sh`.

choices.text: None; all three ran in full
choices.why: The database case could not, and the lesson says so.
